classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate exact positive roots using matching powers.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts evaluate exact positive integer or fractional roots.
questions.methodNote: Identify the nonnegative root by its corresponding power, following Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate exact positive roots using matching powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply matching powers and roots, distinguishing nonnegative even roots from odd roots of negative numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Each part is a matching root and power, including negative bases in d–f.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the power inside the radical and apply the root definition; even roots are nonnegative.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate matching powers while respecting the sign convention for even roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify root bounds by comparing integer, fractional or decimal endpoint powers.

questions.mappingNote: Every part asks for a justification of given root bounds; fractional endpoints require exact comparisons.
questions.methodNote: Compare endpoint powers with the radicand, as in the initial bounds in Example 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justify root bounds by comparing integer, fractional or decimal endpoint powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Locate roots between consecutive natural numbers using matching powers.

questions.mappingNote: The four parts seek the lower natural-number endpoint for square, cube and fourth roots.
questions.methodNote: Place the radicand between consecutive integer powers and take the corresponding roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Locate roots between consecutive natural numbers using matching powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose initial square bounds, retain the correct half after each midpoint test, and decide when the interval establishes rounding, especially near 2.45.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts explicitly require bisection. Part c requires extra iterations because early bounds straddle 2.45.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 repeatedly squares an interval midpoint and retains the appropriate half. Continue until the interval determines rounding to one decimal place.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Repeatedly bisect an interval until both endpoints determine the same one-decimal rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies the taught bisection method to a cube root and establishes one-decimal-place rounding.

questions.mappingNote: The same procedure is applied to the cube root of 2, using cubes instead of squares.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 brackets a root, tests interval midpoints by taking powers, and stops when both bounds round to the same one-decimal-place value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the taught bisection method to a cube root and establishes one-decimal-place rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Squares a sum of roots to identify integer parameters inside a nested radical.

questions.mappingNote: This enrichment question applies that definition after expanding the square of the sum. The expansion itself is not explicitly demonstrated in the inspected 6A teaching.
questions.methodNote: The teaching defines a nonnegative square root by its square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Squares a sum of roots to identify integer parameters inside a nested radical.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses an assumed rational representation to contradict the established irrationality of the square root of 2.

questions.mappingNote: Assuming the translated root is rational gives a rational fraction for the already established irrational root.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 assumes a rational fraction and derives a contradiction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses an assumed rational representation to contradict the established irrationality of the square root of 2.

classification.difficultyReason: Establishes divisibility results by cases and uses them in a lowest-terms contradiction proof.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) establish the divisibility facts required to adapt Example 3 from the square root of 2 to the square root of 3.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 proves irrationality by assuming a fraction in lowest terms and deriving a common factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Establishes divisibility results by cases and uses them in a lowest-terms contradiction proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalises a square-root equation to a symbolic relationship.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a), (b) and (c) successively assess numerical, parameter and general symbolic square-root equations.
questions.methodNote: Use the defining square-root relationship, square nonnegative expressions and rearrange.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises a square-root equation to a symbolic relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Devise an unsignposted digit-count bound that excludes arbitrarily large integers, justify it for all larger digit counts, then exhaust the remaining square candidates.

questions.mappingNote: This enrichment proof extends the taught bounds; no directly matching worked example appears in the inspected teaching.
questions.methodNote: Use square-root bounds and perfect-square structure, followed by finite checking.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a bound for arbitrarily many digits followed by an exhaustive finite check.

classification.difficultyReason: Proves and generalises an identity involving nested higher-order roots.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) uses indices 3 and 4; part (b) generalises the same power-based argument.
questions.methodNote: Raise a nested root to the indicated power and apply the defining nth-root relationship.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves and generalises an identity involving nested higher-order roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify the hinted construction using bounds and irrationality, then extend existence to infinitely many distinct points by constructing suitable rational subintervals.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) constructs an irrational point in an interval; part (b) establishes distinct points in infinitely many disjoint intervals.
questions.methodNote: Use the irrationality of square root 2, proof by contradiction and its positive bounds; apply existence repeatedly to rational subintervals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs irrational numbers and proves their infinitude using rational subintervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify perfect-square or perfect-cube factors, extract their roots, and combine any external coefficient using the taught product rule.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h, j–n extract perfect-square factors; i and o also multiply external coefficients; p–r extract perfect-cube factors. Each is a direct application of the taught product theorem.
questions.methodNote: Theorem 1(a) and Example 1(a), (c), page 6: split a radical into roots of factors and evaluate the perfect root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract perfect-square or perfect-cube factors, including external coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients and radicals, including signed products and higher-order roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c include negative coefficients; b and d–f multiply and simplify square roots; g and h use cube roots; i and j apply the stated general nth-root theorem to fourth roots.
questions.methodNote: Theorem 1(a) and Example 1(b), (d), page 6: multiply external coefficients, combine equal-index roots, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients and radicals, including signed products and higher-order roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the quotient rule with factor extraction; the final fraction also requires recognising that reducing it first exposes perfect squares.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b evaluate perfect square roots in numerator and denominator; c and d evaluate perfect cube roots; e retains an irrational numerator; f and g extract square factors in the numerator; h first reduces the fraction, then applies the quotient rule.
questions.methodNote: Theorem 1(b), page 6: the root of a positive quotient equals the quotient of its roots. Example 1 supplies the factor-extraction method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the quotient rule to square and cube roots of fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare positive surds by expressing each number as a square root.

questions.mappingNote: Each collection directly applies the ordering method of Example 2.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 expresses each positive number as the square root of a natural number and compares radicands.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare positive surds by expressing each number as a square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify square and cube roots, then collect like radical terms.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f collect like radicals; parts g–l first simplify the roots.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 3 extract perfect-power factors using the product rule, then collect like radicals using the distributive law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify square and cube roots, then collect like radical terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise a numerical surd comparison to an inequality with a nonnegative parameter.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the numerical comparison; part b generalises the same method.
questions.methodNote: Express nonnegative quantities as square roots and compare their radicands, following Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise a numerical surd comparison to an inequality with a nonnegative parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Disprove a root-sum identity, determine its equality conditions and prove the corresponding inequality.

questions.mappingNote: Part a tests the limits of root arithmetic; parts b and c analyse the cross term after squaring.
questions.methodNote: Use the product rule for roots and the distributive law; compare squares of nonnegative expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Disprove a root-sum identity, determine its equality conditions and prove the corresponding inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute surd factors, simplify products and collect terms, including subtraction of an entire product.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts assess distributing surd factors and simplifying the resulting sums; expansion is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 Example 1 uses distributive expansion, simplifies root products and collects terms. Page 9 supplies conjugate examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute surd factors, simplify products and collect terms, including subtraction of an entire product.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, simplify surd products and collect rational and irrational terms.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess binomial expansion with surds. Parts c and k are identical in the printed source and are both retained.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 explains the distributive law and demonstrates expansion and root simplification. Page 9 demonstrates difference-of-squares products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets, simplify surd products and collect rational and irrational terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise conjugate products and square their coefficients and radicals correctly; the repeated final factors require ordinary expansion or combining like surds first.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses expansion and simplification of products containing surds.
questions.methodNote: Apply the difference of two squares to conjugate products, as demonstrated in Example 2. Expand the repeated factors in part (l) distributively.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Routine conjugate products, with one repeated-factor exception.

classification.difficultyReason: Form each conjugate by reversing the connecting sign, then apply difference of squares, including squared surd coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess conjugate products rather than denominator rationalisation.
questions.methodNote: Reverse the sign between the terms to obtain the conjugate, then apply the difference of two squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify a conjugate and apply the demonstrated difference-of-squares formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand squared binomials and simplify their middle products, including coefficients and unlike surds.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses squared surd binomials; parts (e) and (g) are independently retained printed duplicates.
questions.methodNote: Use the squared-binomial expansion shown in page 8 Example 1(c), retaining the middle product before simplifying roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand squared binomials and simplify their middle products, including coefficients and unlike surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate nests from the inside, recognise the preserved value, and generalise the scaffolded pattern to other positive values; only a guess is requested for the infinite nest.

questions.mappingNote: The finite evaluations directly assess operations with nested roots; the question itself supplies the pattern-building context for its generalisation.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the innermost radical first, repeatedly use the positive square root of a square, and infer the pattern requested by the question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate nested radicals from the inside and generalise the resulting pattern.

classification.difficultyReason: Use squared-binomial expansions in reverse to recognise nested radicals and determine unknown radicands.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed skill is expansion of surd expressions and its reverse application to nested radicals.
questions.methodNote: Expand a squared sum of roots, then recognise its positive square root. Parts (a–d) build the method used in part (e).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use squared-binomial expansions in reverse to recognise nested radicals and determine unknown radicands.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the squaring hint through nested symbolic radicals, use difference of squares, and justify positivity before recovering roots; then interpret the perfect-square condition and specialise the identities.

questions.mappingNote: This proof task directly applies squared surd-binomial expansion; its definition, hypotheses and hint remain embedded practice content.
questions.methodNote: Follow the embedded hint: square the proposed expressions, use difference of squares to simplify the middle product, then specialise the resulting identities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Prove general nested-root identities, establish rational radicands and specialise the identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate fraction reduction, radical simplification and rationalisation, selecting the appropriate order when a quotient is initially inside a root.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–k rationalise single-radical denominators; l–o apply the quotient rule before simplifying or rationalising.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite a root of a quotient as a quotient of roots; multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's radical, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply single-radical rationalisation and simplify square roots of quotients.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply surd numerators and denominators, evaluate resulting perfect roots, and cancel common factors or matching radicals.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess multiplication of surd fractions; their denominator radicals multiply or cancel to give rational denominators.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerators and denominators, apply square-root multiplication, and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply fractions and simplify products of square roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Use conjugates and expand surd numerators, including fractions with surds in both numerator and denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–g and i–l assess conjugate rationalisation. Part h is an identical nonzero numerator and denominator and simplifies directly to 1.
questions.methodNote: Multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, apply the difference of squares, expand the numerator and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use conjugates and expand surd numerators, including fractions with surds in both numerator and denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Collect and factor linear terms with surd coefficients, then rationalise.

questions.mappingNote: All four equations use the same linear-equation method; rationalising the resulting binomial denominator is the most advanced assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 collects the x terms, factors x, divides by the surd coefficient and rationalises using its conjugate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect and factor linear terms with surd coefficients, then rationalise.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a common denominator and simplify conjugate products.

questions.mappingNote: The explicit common-denominator instruction is retained for each sum or difference; pages 11–12 teach conjugate products and rationalisation.
questions.methodNote: Use a common denominator first, then evaluate the conjugate product by difference of squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a common denominator and simplify conjugate products.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise cancellation across a long sum after rationalising each term.

questions.mappingNote: The finite sum extends the taught conjugate-rationalisation method to consecutive radicands.
questions.methodNote: Multiply by the conjugate to turn each denominator into a difference of squares, then cancel intermediate terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise cancellation across a long sum after rationalising each term.

classification.difficultyReason: Rationalise consecutive even-radicand terms and retain the denominator difference of two.

questions.mappingNote: This sum directly extends conjugate rationalisation, with a factor of one half retained throughout.
questions.methodNote: Multiply each fraction by its conjugate; the difference of consecutive even radicands is two. Cancel intermediate roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rationalise consecutive even-radicand terms and retain the denominator difference of two.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the conjugate denominators, infer that the remaining square root is an integer, and reparameterise the equation to exhibit consecutive natural-number factors.

questions.mappingNote: The proof directly applies algebra with binomial surd denominators.
questions.methodNote: Use conjugates and a common denominator, then identify an integer square root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses a common denominator to deduce an integer factorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Three-term denominators require successive rationalising factors.

questions.mappingNote: Example 3 explicitly demonstrates successive rationalisation of a three-term denominator.
questions.methodNote: Group two denominator terms, multiply by the conjugate, then rationalise the remaining denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Three-term denominators require successive rationalising factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify the supplied cubic identities, map each cube-root denominator to the appropriate identity, and use its quadratic factor to rationalise and simplify.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies the cube-root extension of the conjugate method taught in section 6D; binomial rationalisation is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Expand the supplied cubic identities and use their quadratic factors to obtain rational denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Proves cubic identities and applies them to rationalise cube-root denominators.
